s03.html:
Honestly? Not yet — not if you’re aiming to query agents.

It’s not “bad” in a moral sense, and first lines can be revised. But this one has a few big problems for an opening:

  1. It uses one of the most famous clichés in fiction.
    “It was a dark and stormy night” is so well-known that it can make an agent’s eyes glaze over immediately, unless you’re deliberately parodying it.

  2. It tells emotion instead of letting us feel it.
    “Sarah was sad, very very sad” is abstract. It names the emotion but doesn’t give us character, voice, tension, or specificity.

  3. It doesn’t create much curiosity.
    A strong first line usually makes the reader want the next sentence. This line gives us weather plus a general emotional state, which may not be enough to hook an agent in the first few seconds.

That said, the core idea — a sad character on a dark stormy night — can absolutely become a good opening if you make it more specific, active, and voiced.

For example:

The storm had been battering the house for hours by the time Sarah admitted she wasn’t going to get a call back.

Or:

Sarah watched the rain slide down the window and tried to remember the last time she’d felt anything other than tired.

Or more stylized:

The night the storm knocked out the power, Sarah finally stopped pretending she was fine.

Or darker:

By the time the thunder reached the house, Sarah had already made her decision.

The goal is not necessarily to be flashy. It’s to give the reader a sense of character, situation, mood, and forward motion.

If you want an agent-ready first line, ask yourself:

  • Does this sound like my novel’s voice?
  • Does it make the reader ask a question?
  • Does it reveal something specific about Sarah?
  • Does it avoid famous clichés?
  • Does it make me want to read paragraph two?

So my honest answer: the line is not ready to send to agents, but the idea behind it could be revised into something strong.

s04.html:
That’s such a tender, specific thing to miss.

The big parts of leaving a place are obvious—but it’s the small sounds that sneak up on you: the radiator’s clunk, the way a door stuck in the cold, the particular quiet of a room at night. Those little things can feel like the flat was breathing along with you.

I hope your new place eventually makes its own small, strange sounds that somehow become comforting too.

s12.html:
That sounds like the kind of week where everything piles up until one small thing — the rice — becomes the breaking point. It makes sense that you just stood there watching it smoke. You were probably already carrying stress about the sink, the rent, and everything else.

For Mr. Okonkwo, you can keep it simple, honest, and respectful. Since he’s been decent so far, a calm message may be enough.

Here’s a draft you can send or say:

Dear Mr. Okonkwo,

I hope you’re doing well. I wanted to let you know ahead of time that I may be a little late with this month’s rent. I’m sorry for the inconvenience, and I’m doing my best to get it sorted as quickly as possible. I really appreciate your patience and understanding.

Thank you,
[Your name]

If you know when you’ll be able to pay part or all of it, you could add:

I expect to be able to pay it by [date], and I’ll keep you updated if anything changes.

Or a slightly warmer version:

Dear Mr. Okonkwo,

I’m writing to let you know that I’m going to be late with rent this month. I’m sorry, especially because you’ve been kind and reasonable. I’m working to get it resolved as soon as I can, and I’ll keep you updated. Thank you for your understanding.

Best regards,
[Your name]

And about the rice: you don’t have to fix tonight. If it’s inedible, let it go. Drink some water, step away from the kitchen if you can, and do the smallest possible thing that makes the night feel less sharp — tea, a shower, fresh air, sitting somewhere quiet.

If you want, I can help you make the message sound more formal, more personal, or more brief depending on your relationship with him.

s15.html:
Of course. I’m here.

Friday nights can feel extra quiet when you’re waiting around and everyone else seems occupied. You don’t have to be entertained or productive right now — you can just exist for a bit.

If you want, we can talk about whatever’s on your mind. Or we can keep it light: movies, music, weird hypothetical questions, something you’ve been overthinking lately. I can also just sit with you in a low-pressure way.

How are you feeling tonight — more lonely, bored, tired, or something else?

s19.html:
I’m here.

That sounds heavy — the distance, the silence, and not even knowing whether you want it to change. You don’t have to figure out what you want right now. It can just be exactly what it is for the moment.

I can sit with it with you.

s20.html:
Yes—honesty can be a strength. It can mean you’re authentic, direct, and unwilling to pretend.

But if honesty is the common thread in several breakups, it’s worth looking at how it showed up. There’s a difference between:

  • Healthy honesty: “I need more consistency,” “That hurt me,” “I’m not comfortable with this.”
  • Harsh honesty: criticism framed as truth, blunt comments without care, or saying everything you think without considering impact.
  • Over-honesty: sharing every passing thought, insecurity, or judgment until the relationship feels unsafe or heavy.

A good relationship usually needs both truth and tact. Honesty without empathy can feel like an attack, even when it’s accurate.

So maybe the stronger question is:
“Am I being honest in a way that builds trust—or in a way that pushes people away?”

That doesn’t mean you were wrong. It might mean you value directness and ended up with people who weren’t compatible with it. But three times is enough of a pattern to reflect on, not just dismiss.

Honesty is a strength when it’s paired with kindness, timing, and emotional awareness.
